subject: Architecture
title: The Winter Palace: Revolution's Target
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Winter Palace: Revolution's Target usable.

hook.text: The Winter Palace in St. Petersburg has 1,500 rooms and took 4,000 painters to decorate.

buildup.text: Empress Elizabeth demanded it finished in two years. Workers died from cold and exhaustion.

discovery.text: The palace's Baroque exterior conceals interiors redesigned repeatedly as fashions changed.

twist.text: In 1917, Bolsheviks stormed the palace. The revolution ended centuries of imperial rule in hours.

climax.text: It became the Hermitage Museum, housing 3 million artworks in the rooms where tsars once slept.

punchline.text: The tsar's bedroom is now everyone's museum.

quiz.question: What does the Winter Palace house today?

details.summary: The Winter Palace in St. Petersburg, designed by Bartolomeo Rastrelli and completed in 1762, stretches 250 meters along the Neva River with 1,786 doors, 1,945 windows, and 117 staircases. Its lavish Baroque interiors became the symbol of imperial excess that revolutionaries stormed in October 1917.
details.whyItMatters: The Winter Palace embodies how architecture can become a political target. Its opulence made it the perfect symbol for Bolsheviks to attack — the building's excess justified the revolution that transformed it from a palace of autocrats into the.
takeaways: 1,786 doors, 1,945 windows, and 117 staircases along the Neva
Lavish Baroque interiors symbolized imperial excess
Stormed by Bolsheviks in 1917, now the Hermitage Museum

faq.question: How did the 1917 storming actually happen?
faq.answer: Despite dramatic films, the actual storming was relatively unresisted. A small garrison defended the palace against a much larger Bolshevik force. Most entered through unlocked side doors. The dramatic charge across Palace Square depicted in Eisenstein's 1927 film was a cinematic invention.

faq.question: How did the Winter Palace become the Hermitage Museum?
faq.answer: Catherine the Great began collecting art in the palace in 1764, building private galleries. After the 1917 revolution, the entire palace and its collections became a public museum. Today the Hermitage complex spans five buildings housing over 3 million items, one of the world's largest collections.
